title: Τηλεμάχου ἄφιξις
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Eumaeus finishes the story of how he came to Ithaca. The Phoenician traders spent a year with his father’s household; the Phoenician woman of his father’s house slips away with them, taking the boy and three goblets stolen from the hall. On the seventh day at sea Artemis struck the woman dead and she was thrown overboard; the traders sold the boy to Laertes. Odysseus, still unrecognised, answers that Eumaeus has a kind master and a good life beside his sorrows, while he himself is a wanderer. At dawn Telemachus’s ship puts in on the coast of Ithaca. He sends his crew on to the town and says he will go to the farms. His guest Theoclymenus asks where he is to go; Telemachus names Eurymachus, the leading suitor, as a host. A falcon, Apollo’s messenger, flies up on the right with a dove in its talons and drops feathers between the ship and Telemachus; Theoclymenus reads it as a sign that Telemachus’s house will always rule. Telemachus gives his guest into the care of his companion Peiraeus, the crew sail off, and Telemachus goes on foot to the swineherd’s yard.

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ἀπέβη πρὸς δώματα καλά,
οἱ δ’ ἐνιαυτὸν ἅπαντα παρ’ ἡμῖν αὖθι μένοντες
ἐν νηῒ γλαφυρῇ βίοτον πολὺν ἐμπολόωντο.
sentences.tr:
hē men ar’ hōs eipous’ apebē pros dōmata kala,
hoi d’ eniauton hapanta par’ hēmin authi menontes
en nēï glaphyrēi bioton polyn empoloōnto.
sentences.l:
She, indeed, then so having spoken went away to the fair halls,
and they for a whole year with us right there staying
in the hollow ship a great livelihood were trading-for.
sentences.i: So she spoke and went away to the fair halls, and the men stayed on with us right there for a whole year, getting a great livelihood by trade in their hollow ship.
sentences.n: Eumaeus’s speech, which opened at 15.390 in the previous part, runs straight on here, so this unit has no opening quotation mark: the woman has just finished speaking to the sailors, and ἡ μὲν … ἀπέβη 'she, for her part, went away' reports her leaving. εἰποῦσ’ is the aorist participle of εἶπον with its -α elided. The halls are the house of Eumaeus’s father (see 15.459). οἱ δ’ 'but they' are the sailors; ἐνιαυτὸν ἅπαντα 'the whole year' is an accusative of duration; αὖθι 'right there'; μένοντες is a participle 'staying'. γλαφυρῇ 'hollow' comes from γλάφω 'hollow out'; it and κοίλη in the next unit are both 'hollow'. ἐμπολόωντο is the uncontracted imperfect middle of ἐμπολάω 'get by trading', and βίοτον πολὺν is 'a great livelihood', that is, plenty to live on.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ κοίλη νηῦς ἤχθετο τοῖσι νέεσθαι,
καὶ τότ’ ἄρ’ ἄγγελον ἧκαν, ὃς ἀγγείλειε γυναικί.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē koilē nēus ēchtheto toisi neesthai,
kai tot’ ar’ angelon hēkan, hos angeileie gynaiki.
sentences.l:
But when indeed the hollow ship was loaded, for them to go home,
then thereupon a messenger they sent, who should tell the woman.
sentences.i: But when the hollow ship was loaded for their voyage home, they sent a messenger to bring word to the woman.
sentences.n: κοίλη νηῦς is 'the hollow ship' (νηῦς is the Homeric nominative of ναῦς). ἤχθετο is the imperfect of ἄχθομαι, which usually means 'be vexed'; said of a ship it is taken to mean 'was weighed down, was loaded', from ἄχθος 'load'. That is the traditional sense, and the construction with τοῖσι νέεσθαι 'for them to go home' (νέεσθαι is the uncontracted infinitive of νέομαι 'go, return') is unusual. καὶ τότ’ ἄρ’ 'and then, thereupon'. ἧκαν is the aorist of ἵημι 'send'. ὃς ἀγγείλειε is a relative clause of purpose with the aorist optative, 'who should bring word'; γυναικί 'to the woman' is the Phoenician woman of Eumaeus’s story.

sentences.t:
ἤλυθ’ ἀνὴρ πολύϊδρις ἐμοῦ πρὸς δώματα πατρὸς
χρύσεον ὅρμον ἔχων, μετὰ δ’ ἠλέκτροισιν ἔερτο.
sentences.tr:
ēlyth’ anēr polyïdris emou pros dōmata patros
chryseon hormon echōn, meta d’ ēlektroisin eerto.
sentences.l:
Came a much-knowing man to my father’s halls,
a golden necklace having, and amid it with amber beads it was strung.
sentences.i: A man who knew a great deal came to my father’s house with a golden necklace, strung with beads of amber.
sentences.n: ἤλυθ’ is ἤλυθε, the epic form of Attic ἦλθε, aorist of ἔρχομαι. πολύϊδρις 'much-knowing' joins πολύς 'much' to ἴδρις 'knowing, skilled' (from the root of οἶδα). ἐμοῦ … πατρός is 'of me, of father', that is 'my father’s': the speaker is Eumaeus, and these halls are his father’s. ὅρμον here is 'necklace' (not the ὅρμον 'anchorage' of 497). ἠλέκτροισιν is a dative plural of ἤλεκτρον 'amber' (the word can also name the alloy electrum; amber is the usual sense of the beads on a necklace). ἔερτο is the epic pluperfect passive of εἴρω 'string': the necklace 'was strung' (a pluperfect of state) with amber among the gold, μετά 'among'.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἄρ’ ἐν μεγάρῳ δμῳαὶ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ
χερσίν τ’ ἀμφαφόωντο καὶ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ὁρῶντο,
ὦνον ὑπισχόμεναι·
sentences.tr:
ton men ar’ en megarōi dmōiai kai potnia mētēr
chersin t’ amphaphoōnto kai ophthalmoisin horōnto,
ōnon hypischomenai·
sentences.i: In the hall the maids and my lady mother handled it and looked it over, offering a price;
sentences.n: τὸν is the pronoun 'it', the necklace (ὅρμος is masculine). δμῳαί 'maidservants' and πότνια μήτηρ 'the lady mother' (that is, Eumaeus’s mother) are the women of the house. ἀμφαφόωντο and ὁρῶντο are imperfects: the first is the uncontracted form of ἀμφαφάομαι 'feel all over, handle', the second is ὁράω in the middle, 'look at, examine'; χερσίν and ὀφθαλμοῖσιν are datives 'with hands, with eyes'. ὑπισχόμεναι is the present participle of ὑπισχνέομαι 'promise, offer', and ὦνον 'price'. The unit stops in the middle of line 463.

sentences.t: ὁ δὲ τῇ κατένευσε σιωπῇ.
sentences.tr: ho de tēi kateneuse siōpēi.
sentences.l: and he to her nodded in silence.
sentences.i: but he nodded to her in silence.
sentences.n: ὁ and τῇ are pronouns: 'he', the trader, and 'to her', the woman of line 458. κατένευσε is the aorist of κατανεύω 'nod assent'; σιωπῇ is a dative of manner, 'in silence'. The nod is the signal passed to her while the others are busy with the necklace. The unit begins in the middle of line 463.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι ὁ καννεύσας κοίλην ἐπὶ νῆα βεβήκει,
ἡ δ’ ἐμὲ χειρὸς ἑλοῦσα δόμων ἐξῆγε θύραζε.
sentences.tr:
ē toi ho kanneusas koilēn epi nēa bebēkei,
hē d’ eme cheiros helousa domōn exēge thyraze.
sentences.l:
Truly he, having nodded, to the hollow ship had gone,
and she me by the hand having taken led out of the house to the door.
sentences.i: He, for his part, having given the nod, had gone off to the hollow ship, and she took me by the hand and led me out of the house, out of doors.
sentences.n: ἦ τοι 'truly' and the pair ὁ … ἡ δ’ 'he … she' set the two movements side by side. καννεύσας is the printed form of κατανεύσας (the verb of the nod in the previous unit), the preverb shortened and assimilated: κατα- loses its final α and the τ becomes ν. βεβήκει is the unaugmented pluperfect of βαίνω, 'had gone', that is 'was on his way'. χειρὸς ἑλοῦσα is a genitive of the part taken hold of with the aorist participle of αἱρέω, 'having taken (me) by the hand'. ἐξῆγε is the imperfect of ἐξάγω; δόμων is a genitive of separation after ἐξ- in ἐξῆγε, 'out of the house'; θύραζε has the suffix -ζε, like -δε, 'to the door, out of doors'.

sentences.t:
εὗρε δ’ ἐνὶ προδόμῳ ἠμὲν δέπα ἠδὲ τραπέζας
ἀνδρῶν δαιτυμόνων, οἵ μευ πατέρ’ ἀμφεπένοντο.
sentences.tr:
heure d’ eni prodomōi ēmen depa ēde trapezas
andrōn daitymonōn, hoi meu pater’ amphepenonto.
sentences.l:
And she found in the fore-house both cups and tables
of feasting men, who my father were attending.
sentences.i: In the vestibule she found both the cups and the tables of the men feasting there, who were in attendance on my father.
sentences.n: The subject of εὗρε is the woman. προδόμῳ is the dative of πρόδομος, the 'fore-house', the vestibule in front of the main hall. ἠμὲν … ἠδὲ 'both … and' is the epic form of τε … καί. δέπα is the plural of δέπας 'cup'. δαιτυμόνων is a genitive plural of δαιτυμών 'feaster, one who dines', in apposition to ἀνδρῶν. οἵ μευ πατέρ’ ἀμφεπένοντο is a relative clause: μευ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ, 'my', and ἀμφεπένοντο the imperfect of ἀμφιπένομαι 'busy oneself about, attend to'.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἄρ’ ἐς θῶκον πρόμολον, δήμοιό τε φῆμιν,
ἡ δ’ αἶψα τρί’ ἄλεισα κατακρύψασ’ ὑπὸ κόλπῳ
ἔκφερεν·
sentences.tr:
hoi men ar’ es thōkon promolon, dēmoio te phēmin,
hē d’ aipsa tri’ aleisa katakrypsas’ hypo kolpōi
ekpheren·
sentences.i: The men went off to the seat of council and the talk of the people, and she quickly hid three goblets in the fold of her dress and carried them out;
sentences.n: οἱ μὲν … ἡ δ’ again sets 'they' against 'she'. πρόμολον is the unaugmented aorist of προβλώσκω 'go forth'. θῶκος is 'a seat', here the place where the men sit to talk; δήμοιο is the epic genitive of δῆμος 'people' and φῆμις is 'talk, report'. The two accusatives ἐς θῶκον and δήμοιό τε φῆμιν are read as two goals of the same movement, the place of meeting and the talk there; the exact sense of φῆμιν here is not certain. ἄλεισα is the plural of ἄλεισον 'goblet'; κατακρύψασ’ is the aorist participle of κατακρύπτω 'hide away'; κόλπῳ is 'bosom', the fold of the dress over the girdle, where she hides the stolen goblets. ἔκφερεν is the imperfect of ἐκφέρω 'carry out'. The unit ends in the middle of line 470.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἑπόμην ἀεσιφροσύνῃσι.
sentences.tr: autar egōn hepomēn aesiphrosynēisi.
sentences.l: but I was following in witlessness.
sentences.i: and I, in my witlessness, followed.
sentences.n: ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ and ἑπόμην the imperfect of ἕπομαι 'follow'. ἀεσιφροσύνῃσι is a dative plural in -ῃσι of ἀεσιφροσύνη 'witlessness, folly'; the plural of an abstract noun names a state, 'in witlessness'. The first element ἀεσι- is of unknown origin, so the word is known only from its sense in use: lack of understanding, here a child’s. The unit begins in the middle of line 470.

sentences.t: δύσετό τ’ ἠέλιος, σκιόωντό τε πᾶσαι ἀγυιαί·
sentences.tr: dyseto t’ ēelios, skioōnto te pasai aguiai·
sentences.l: And the sun set, and all the streets grew shadowy.
sentences.i: The sun set, and all the streets grew dark.
sentences.n: δύσετο is the unaugmented aorist middle of δύω 'sink, set'; σκιόωντο is the uncontracted imperfect (diectasis) of σκιάω 'grow dark, lie in shadow', and ἀγυιαί are 'streets'. The same line is used elsewhere in the poem for the fall of evening; it ends here with a raised dot, and the English has a semicolon.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δ’ ἐς λιμένα κλυτὸν ἤλθομεν ὦκα κιόντες,
ἔνθ’ ἄρα Φοινίκων ἀνδρῶν ἦν ὠκύαλος νηῦς.
sentences.tr:
hēmeis d’ es limena klyton ēlthomen ōka kiontes,
enth’ ara Phoinikōn andrōn ēn ōkyalos nēus.
sentences.l:
and we to the famous harbour came, quickly going,
where then of the Phoenician men was the swift-sailing ship.
sentences.i: and we came quickly to the famous harbour, where the swift-sailing ship of the Phoenician men lay.
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς 'we' are Eumaeus and the woman. κιόντες is the participle of κίω 'go'; ὦκα 'quickly'. κλυτόν 'famous' is the ordinary epic adjective. ἔνθ’ ἄρα 'where then'. Φοινίκων ἀνδρῶν is a genitive of possession, 'of the Phoenician men', and ὠκύαλος 'swift on the sea' joins ὠκύς 'swift' to ἅλς 'sea'.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἀναβάντες ἐπέπλεον ὑγρὰ κέλευθα,
νὼ ἀναβησάμενοι·
sentences.tr:
hoi men epeit’ anabantes epepleon hygra keleutha,
nō anabēsamenoi·
sentences.l:
They then, having embarked, sailed over the watery ways,
us two having taken aboard;
sentences.i: The Phoenicians then went aboard and sailed over the watery ways, taking the two of us on board;
sentences.n: ἐπέπλεον ὑγρὰ κέλευθα is 'sailed over the watery ways': ἐπιπλέω takes an accusative of the sea passed over; ὑγρά 'wet, watery'; κέλευθα is the epic neuter plural of κέλευθος 'way, path'. ἀναβάντες is the aorist participle of ἀναβαίνω 'go up, go aboard'. νώ is the dual 'we two' (the woman and the boy), and ἀναβησάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ἀναβαίνω used causatively, 'having made (us) go aboard'. The unit ends in the middle of line 475.

sentences.t: ἐπὶ δὲ Ζεὺς οὖρον ἴαλλεν.
sentences.tr: epi de Zeus ouron iallen.
sentences.l: and upon them Zeus a fair wind sent.
sentences.i: and Zeus sent them a fair wind.
sentences.n: ἐπί … ἴαλλεν is tmesis for ἐπιίαλλεν 'sent upon'; ἐπί stands alone with 'them' understood. ἴαλλεν is the imperfect of ἰάλλω 'send, hurl'. οὖρον is the accusative of οὖρος 'fair wind' (a different word from οὖρος 'guard'). The unit begins in the middle of line 475.

sentences.t: ἑξῆμαρ μὲν ὁμῶς πλέομεν νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ·
sentences.tr: hexēmar men homōs pleomen nyktas te kai ēmar·
sentences.l: Six days alike we sailed, both nights and day;
sentences.i: For six days and nights together we sailed on;
sentences.n: ἑξῆμαρ 'for six days' is an adverb built from ἕξ 'six' and ἦμαρ 'day'. ὁμῶς 'alike, together'; νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ 'both nights and day' sets the plural 'nights' beside the singular 'day'. The line is found elsewhere in the poem, with the same English.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ ἕβδομον ἦμαρ ἐπὶ Ζεὺς θῆκε Κρονίων,
τὴν μὲν ἔπειτα γυναῖκα βάλ’ Ἄρτεμις ἰοχέαιρα,
ἄντλῳ δ’ ἐνδούπησε πεσοῦσ’ ὡς εἰναλίη κήξ.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē hebdomon ēmar epi Zeus thēke Kroniōn,
tēn men epeita gynaika bal’ Artemis iocheaira,
antlōi d’ endoupēse pesous’ hōs einaliē kēx.
sentences.l:
But when indeed the seventh day Zeus set on, the son of Cronus,
that woman then struck Artemis, the arrow-pourer,
and she thudded in the bilge, having fallen, like a sea-dwelling kex.
sentences.i: But when Zeus, the son of Cronus, added the seventh day, then Artemis, who showers her arrows, struck the woman, and she fell with a thud into the bilge like a sea-bird.
sentences.n: ἐπὶ … θῆκε is tmesis for ἐπέθηκε 'added'; the first line is found elsewhere in the poem. τὴν μὲν … γυναῖκα 'that woman' is the Phoenician woman; her sudden death is put down to Artemis, and the shot is plain: βάλ’ is βάλε, the unaugmented aorist of βάλλω 'strike, hit'. ἰοχέαιρα 'arrow-pourer' is Artemis’s epithet; its second element is disputed, χέω 'pour' or χαίρω 'delight in', so the sense is either 'who showers arrows' or 'who delights in arrows'. ἄντλῳ is the dative of ἄντλος 'bilge, the water in the hold'. ἐνδούπησε is the aorist of ἐνδουπέω 'fall with a thud'; πεσοῦσ’ is the aorist participle of πίπτω. εἰναλίη is ἐναλίη 'of the sea' with its first syllable lengthened. κήξ is a sea-bird of unidentified kind (gull, tern, shearwater and cormorant have all been proposed); only its being a sea-bird is certain, and the point of the comparison is a body dropping into the water.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὴν μὲν φώκῃσι καὶ ἰχθύσι κύρμα γενέσθαι
ἔκβαλον·
sentences.tr:
kai tēn men phōkēisi kai ichthysi kyrma genesthai
ekbalon·
sentences.l:
And her to seals and to fishes prey to become
they threw out;
sentences.i: and they threw her out to become prey for seals and fishes;
sentences.n: τὴν μὲν 'her' picks up the woman. φώκῃσι and ἰχθύσι are datives 'for seals, for fishes' with γενέσθαι 'to become'; κύρμα 'prey, a thing come upon', is from κύρω 'meet with'. ἔκβαλον is the unaugmented aorist of ἐκβάλλω 'throw out'; the sailors are the subject but are not named. The body is thrown overboard. The unit ends in the middle of line 481.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ λιπόμην ἀκαχήμενος ἦτορ·
τοὺς δ’ Ἰθάκῃ ἐπέλασσε φέρων ἄνεμός τε καὶ ὕδωρ,
ἔνθα με Λαέρτης πρίατο κτεάτεσσιν ἑοῖσιν.
sentences.tr:
autar egō lipomēn akachēmenos ētor·
tous d’ Ithakēi epelasse pherōn anemos te kai hydōr,
entha me Laertēs priato kteatessin heoisin.
sentences.i: but I was left behind, grieved at heart; and the wind and the water carried them on and brought them near to Ithaca, where Laertes bought me with his own possessions.
sentences.n: λιπόμην is the aorist of λείπω in the middle with a passive sense, 'I was left behind'. ἀκαχήμενος is the perfect participle middle of ἀκαχίζω 'distress', 'grieved'; ἦτορ is an accusative of respect, 'in heart'. τοὺς 'them' is the ship’s company, Eumaeus among them. ἐπέλασσε is the aorist of πελάζω 'bring near', with the dative Ἰθάκῃ 'to Ithaca'; its subject is the two nouns ἄνεμός τε καὶ ὕδωρ 'wind and water', with the singular verb agreeing with the first; φέρων 'carrying' agrees with ἄνεμος. ἔνθα 'where'. πρίατο is the unaugmented aorist middle of πρίαμαι 'buy'; κτεάτεσσιν is the dative plural in -εσσι of κτέαρ 'possession', here 'with his possessions' as the price; ἑοῖσιν is the possessive 'his own'.

sentences.t: οὕτω τήνδε τε γαῖαν ἐγὼν ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσι.
sentences.tr: houtō tēnde te gaian egōn idon ophthalmoisi.
sentences.l: And thus this land I saw with my eyes.”
sentences.i: That is how I came to see this land with my own eyes.”
sentences.n: This unit ends Eumaeus’s speech, which began at 15.390 in the previous part; the closing quotation mark is here. οὕτω 'thus'; τήνδε 'this', the land he is standing in; τε joins the sentence to the story before it ('and so'). ἐγών is the epic ἐγώ and ἴδον the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω (Attic εἶδον); ὀφθαλμοῖσι is a dative plural in -οισι, 'with my eyes'.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ διογενὴς Ὀδυσεὺς ἠμείβετο μύθῳ·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au diogenēs Odyseus ēmeibeto mythōi·
sentences.l: Him in turn Zeus-sprung Odysseus answered with a word:
sentences.i: Then Zeus-born Odysseus answered him in turn:
sentences.n: This is a reply-formula. τὸν 'him' is a pronoun, αὖ 'in turn', ἠμείβετο the imperfect middle of ἀμείβομαι 'answer', and μύθῳ the dative 'with a word'. διογενής 'Zeus-sprung' joins Zeus (Διός) to the root of γίγνομαι 'be born' and is a standing epithet of Odysseus; it is translated each time. The name is spelled Ὀδυσεύς with one σ here, as the metre requires, beside Ὀδυσσῆος in lines 522 and 554. Odysseus is still unrecognised.

sentences.t:
Εὔμαι’, ἦ μάλα δή μοι ἐνὶ φρεσὶ θυμὸν ὄρινας
ταῦτα ἕκαστα λέγων, ὅσα δὴ πάθες ἄλγεα θυμῷ.
sentences.tr:
Eumai’, ē mala dē moi eni phresi thymon orinas
tauta hekasta legōn, hosa dē pathes algea thymōi.
sentences.l:
“Eumaeus, truly very much indeed in my mind my heart you stirred
all these things one by one telling, as many pains as you suffered in heart.
sentences.i: “Eumaeus, you have truly stirred the heart in my mind by telling me each of these things, all the pains that you suffered in your heart.
sentences.n: Odysseus answers; the speech runs to line 492. Εὔμαι’ is the vocative Εὔμαιε with its -ε elided. ἦ μάλα δή 'truly, very much, indeed' strengthens the statement. μοι is a dative of the person affected, 'in me'; ἐνὶ φρεσί 'in the mind' (φρένες are the seat of thought and feeling); θυμὸν ὄρινας is 'you stirred my heart', the aorist of ὀρίνω 'stir, rouse'. ταῦτα ἕκαστα 'each of these things' is the object of λέγων 'telling'. πάθες is the unaugmented aorist of πάσχω (Attic ἔπαθες) and ἄλγεα 'pains' its object with ὅσα 'as many … as'; θυμῷ 'in your heart'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι σοὶ μὲν παρὰ καὶ κακῷ ἐσθλὸν ἔθηκε
Ζεύς, ἐπεὶ ἀνδρὸς δώματ’ ἀφίκεο πολλὰ μογήσας
ἠπίου, ὃς δή τοι παρέχει βρῶσίν τε πόσιν τε
ἐνδυκέως, ζώεις δ’ ἀγαθὸν βίον·
sentences.tr:
all’ ē toi soi men para kai kakōi esthlon ethēke
Zeus, epei andros dōmat’ aphikeo polla mogēsas
ēpiou, hos dē toi parechei brōsin te posin te
endykeōs, zōeis d’ agathon bion·
sentences.l:
But truly to you, beside even evil, a good thing set
Zeus, since a man’s halls you reached, having toiled much,
of a kind one, who indeed provides you with food and drink
kindly, and you live a good life;
sentences.i: But still, Zeus has set some good beside the evil for you, since after all your toil you have come to the house of a gentle man, who kindly provides you with food and drink; and you live a good life;
sentences.n: παρά 'beside' stands before καὶ κακῷ and can be read with that dative ('beside even evil', as in l and i) or as tmesis with ἔθηκε ('set beside'); the sense is the same. ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι 'but still, truly'. σοὶ μέν 'to you, for your part' is answered by αὐτὰρ ἐγώ γε 'but I, for my part' in the next unit. κακῷ and ἐσθλόν are adjectives used as nouns, 'the evil' and 'a good thing'. ἀφίκεο is the aorist middle of ἀφικνέομαι with the uncontracted ending -εο (Attic -ου); πολλὰ μογήσας 'having toiled much' is an aorist participle of μογέω. ἠπίου 'kind, gentle' is a genitive agreeing with ἀνδρός; the house is the house of a man who treats his people well. παρέχει 'provides', βρῶσίν τε πόσιν τε 'both food and drink', ἐνδυκέως 'kindly'. ζώεις is the uncontracted form of ζῇς 'you live'. The unit ends in the middle of line 491.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγώ γε
πολλὰ βροτῶν ἐπὶ ἄστε’ ἀλώμενος ἐνθάδ’ ἱκάνω.
sentences.tr:
autar egō ge
polla brotōn epi aste’ alōmenos enthad’ hikanō.
sentences.l:
but I, at least,
over many cities of mortals wandering, to here come.”
sentences.i: but I, for my part, have wandered over many cities of mortals and have come here.”
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐγώ γε 'but I, for my part' answers σοὶ μέν of line 488, setting Odysseus’s lot against Eumaeus’s. ἄστε’ is ἄστεα, the neuter plural of ἄστυ 'city, town'; πολλά … ἄστεα 'many cities'; βροτῶν 'of mortals'. ἀλώμενος is the participle of ἀλάομαι 'wander'; ἱκάνω 'I come, arrive' is a present with the sense 'I have come'. The closing quotation mark of Odysseus’s speech is here. The unit begins in the middle of line 491.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον,
καδδραθέτην δ’ οὐ πολλὸν ἐπὶ χρόνον, ἀλλὰ μίνυνθα·
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi men toiauta pros allēlous agoreuon,
kaddrathetēn d’ ou pollon epi chronon, alla minyntha·
sentences.l:
So they, such things to one another were saying,
and the two fell asleep for no long time, but a little;
sentences.i: So they talked in this way with one another, and the two slept for no long time, but only a little;
sentences.n: Murray begins a new paragraph; the first line is found elsewhere in the poem with the same English. ἀγόρευον is the imperfect of ἀγορεύω 'speak'; τοιαῦτα 'such things'. καδδραθέτην is the dual aorist of καταδαρθάνω 'fall asleep', the τ of κατα- assimilated to the δ that follows (κατ-δραθ- becomes καδ-δραθ-); the dual 'the two' is the two men in the hut, Odysseus and Eumaeus. οὐ πολλὸν ἐπὶ χρόνον 'for not much time'; ἀλλά 'but'; μίνυνθα 'for a little while', an adverb.

sentences.t: αἶψα γὰρ Ἠὼς ἦλθεν ἐΰθρονος.
sentences.tr: aipsa gar Ēōs ēlthen eÿthronos.
sentences.l: for soon Dawn came, fair-throned.
sentences.i: for fair-throned Dawn soon came.
sentences.n: γάρ 'for' explains why their sleep was short. αἶψα 'quickly, soon'; Ἠώς 'Dawn'; ἐΰθρονος 'fair-throned', her standing epithet, translated each time. The unit is the first part of line 495, ending at the full stop before οἱ δ’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐπὶ χέρσου
Τηλεμάχου ἕταροι λύον ἱστία, κὰδ δ’ ἕλον ἱστὸν
καρπαλίμως, τὴν δ’ εἰς ὅρμον προέρυσσαν ἐρετμοῖς·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ epi chersou
Tēlemachou hetaroi lyon histia, kad d’ helon histon
karpalimōs, tēn d’ eis hormon proeryssan eretmois·
sentences.i: and at the shore Telemachus’ companions loosed the sails, took the mast down quickly, and pulled her on into the anchorage with oars;
sentences.n: The scene turns to the ship that carried Telemachus. οἱ δ’ 'and they' are Telemachus’s crew, as Τηλεμάχου ἕταροι 'Telemachus’s companions' says (ἕταροι is the short form of ἑταῖροι). ἐπὶ χέρσου 'on the dry land' is ἐπί with the genitive; it says where they are, near the shore, without saying whether the keel has touched. λύον ἱστία 'loosed the sails' is to let them down. κὰδ δ’ ἕλον ἱστὸν is tmesis (κατὰ … ἕλον 'took down'); ἱστός here is the mast, the same word as 'loom' at 517 (something set upright, from ἵστημι). τὴν is the ship. ὅρμον here is the anchorage, not the ὅρμον 'necklace' of 460. προέρυσσαν is an aorist of προερύω 'drag forward'; ἐρετμοῖς 'with oars'. The unit begins in the middle of line 495.

sentences.t: ἐκ δ’ εὐνὰς ἔβαλον, κατὰ δὲ πρυμνήσι’ ἔδησαν·
sentences.tr: ek d’ eunas ebalon, kata de prymnēsi’ edēsan·
sentences.l: and out they threw the anchor-stones, and down they bound the stern-cables;
sentences.i: they cast out the anchor-stones and made fast the stern-cables;
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἔβαλον and κατὰ … ἔδησαν are both tmesis: ἐκβάλλω 'throw out' and καταδέω 'bind down, make fast'. εὐνάς, the accusative of εὐναί, means here 'anchor-stones', the weights thrown over the bow; the same word elsewhere means 'beds'. πρυμνήσι’ is the elided plural of πρυμνήσιον 'stern-cable', the rope that holds the stern to the shore.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ βαῖνον ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης,
δεῖπνόν τ’ ἐντύνοντο κερῶντό τε αἴθοπα οἶνον.
sentences.tr:
ek de kai autoi bainon epi rhēgmini thalassēs,
deipnon t’ entynonto kerōnto te aithopa oinon.
sentences.l:
and out also themselves they stepped upon the surf-line of the sea,
and a meal they prepared and mixed the fire-faced wine.
sentences.i: and they themselves stepped out onto the shore where the sea breaks, and got a meal ready and mixed the wine that has the look of fire.
sentences.n: ἐκ … βαῖνον is tmesis, 'were stepping out'; καὶ αὐτοί 'they themselves, too' (after the gear). ῥηγμῖνι is the dative of ῥηγμίν 'the place where the sea breaks', the surf-line. ἐντύνοντο 'were making ready (for themselves)' and κερῶντο 'were mixing' are imperfects middle; κερῶντο is the contracted form of κεράοντο (κεράομαι), the wine being mixed with water. αἴθοπα οἶνον 'fire-faced wine' is the stock epithet of wine (αἴθω 'burn' + ὄψ 'look, face'), translated each time.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
τοῖσι δὲ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἤρχετο μύθων·
sentences.tr:
autar epei posios kai edētyos ex eron hento,
toisi de Tēlemachos pepnymenos ērcheto mythōn·
sentences.l:
But when of drink and of food they had put away desire,
and among them prudent Telemachus began to speak:
sentences.i: But when they had put from them the desire for drink and food, prudent Telemachus began to speak among them:
sentences.n: Both lines are formulas found elsewhere in the poem, the first closing a meal and the second opening a speech, and the English is the same each time. πόσιος and ἐδητύος are genitives of πόσις 'drink' and ἐδητύς 'food'; ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο is tmesis for ἐξέντο, the aorist middle of ἐξίημι 'send out', 'put away from themselves', with ἔρον 'desire' (ἔρος). τοῖσι 'among them' is a dative pronoun; πεπνυμένος 'prudent' is Telemachus’s standing epithet; ἤρχετο μύθων 'began the words', a genitive after ἄρχω.

sentences.t:
ὑμεῖς μὲν νῦν ἄστυδ’ ἐλαύνετε νῆα μέλαιναν,
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἀγροὺς ἐπιείσομαι ἠδὲ βοτῆρας·
sentences.tr:
hymeis men nyn astyd’ elaunete nēa melainan,
autar egōn agrous epieisomai ēde botēras·
sentences.l:
“You now to the town drive the black ship,
but I to the fields will go, and to the herdsmen;
sentences.i: “Now you, take the black ship on to the town; but I will go to the fields and to the herdsmen;
sentences.n: Telemachus speaks to his crew; the speech runs to line 507. ὑμεῖς 'you' is plural. ἄστυδ’ is ἄστυδε, with the suffix -δε, 'to the town'; ἐλαύνετε 'drive' is an imperative, here of rowing the ship on; νῆα μέλαιναν 'the black ship', νῆα being the accusative of νηῦς. ἐπιείσομαι is the future middle of ἔπειμι 'go to'; ἀγρούς 'fields, farms'; βοτῆρας 'herdsmen', from βόσκω 'feed, graze'.

sentences.t: ἑσπέριος δ’ εἰς ἄστυ ἰδὼν ἐμὰ ἔργα κάτειμι.
sentences.tr: hesperios d’ eis asty idōn ema erga kateimi.
sentences.l: and in the evening to the town, having seen my works, I shall go down.
sentences.i: and in the evening, when I have looked over my cultivated land, I will come down to the town.
sentences.n: ἑσπέριος 'in the evening' is an adjective where English uses an adverb. ἰδών is the aorist participle of ὁράω 'having seen'. ἔργα 'works' here is the work of the fields, his cultivated land, as in ἀγρούς of the line before. κάτειμι is 'I shall go down', from κατά + εἶμι, the verb of going down to the town.

sentences.t:
ἠῶθεν δέ κεν ὔμμιν ὁδοιπόριον παραθείμην,
δαῖτ’ ἀγαθὴν κρειῶν τε καὶ οἴνου ἡδυπότοιο.
sentences.tr:
ēōthen de ken ymmin hodoiporion paratheimēn,
dait’ agathēn kreiōn te kai oinou hēdypotoio.
sentences.l:
and at dawn to you I would set beside a road-provision,
a good feast of meats and of sweet-to-drink wine.”
sentences.i: and at dawn I would set before you provisions for the road, a good feast of meat and wine sweet to drink.”
sentences.n: ἠῶθεν 'at dawn' has the suffix -θεν (compare οἶκόθεν 'from home'), here marking time. κε with the optative παραθείμην (aorist middle of παρατίθημι 'set before') makes 'I would set before'; ὔμμιν is the epic form of ὑμῖν 'for you'. ὁδοιπόριον 'provisions for the road' is explained by δαῖτ’ ἀγαθήν 'a good feast' in apposition. κρειῶν is the uncontracted genitive plural of κρέας 'meat', and οἴνου ἡδυπότοιο 'wine sweet to drink' (ἡδύποτος) is a second genitive after δαῖτα. The closing quotation mark of Telemachus’s speech is here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε Θεοκλύμενος θεοειδής·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe Theoklymenos theoeidēs·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Theoclymenus, godlike-in-form:
sentences.i: Then Theoclymenus, godlike in form, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: This is the reply-formula for Theoclymenus. τὸν 'him' is Telemachus; αὖτε 'in turn'; προσέειπε is the aorist of προσεῖπον 'speak to, address'. θεοειδής 'godlike in form' joins θεός 'god' to εἶδος 'form, look' and is Theoclymenus’s standing epithet, translated each time.

sentences.t: πῆ γὰρ ἐγώ, φίλε τέκνον, ἴω;
sentences.tr: pē gar egō, phile teknon, iō;
sentences.l: “For where, I, dear child, am I to go?
sentences.i: “For where am I to go, my dear child?
sentences.n: Theoclymenus answers with three questions; the speech runs to line 511. πῆ 'where (to)?'; ἐγώ 'I' is set in front for emphasis; φίλε τέκνον 'dear child' is a kindly address to a younger man; ἴω is the subjunctive of εἶμι 'go', in a deliberative question, 'am I to go?'. The unit ends in the middle of line 509.

sentences.t:
τεῦ δώμαθ’ ἵκωμαι
ἀνδρῶν οἳ κραναὴν Ἰθάκην κάτα κοιρανέουσιν;
sentences.tr:
teu dōmath’ hikōmai
andrōn hoi kranaēn Ithakēn kata koiraneousin;
sentences.l:
To whose halls am I to come
of the men who rocky Ithaca throughout play the lord?
sentences.i: To whose house am I to come, of the men who lord it throughout rocky Ithaca?
sentences.n: τεῦ is the Ionic genitive of τίς 'whose?'; δώμαθ’ is δώματα, the plural of δῶμα used of a single house; ἵκωμαι is the aorist subjunctive of ἱκνέομαι 'come to', again deliberative. κραναὴν Ἰθάκην κάτα: κάτα is κατά placed after its noun, 'throughout rocky Ithaca', and κραναή 'rocky' is Ithaca’s standing epithet. κοιρανέουσιν is from κοίρανος 'ruler'; the verb here says only that these men hold power in the island. The unit begins in the middle of line 509.

sentences.t: ἦ ἰθὺς σῆς μητρὸς ἴω καὶ σοῖο δόμοιο;
sentences.tr: ē ithys sēs mētros iō kai soio domoio;
sentences.l: Is it straight to your mother and to your house that I am to go?”
sentences.i: Am I to go straight to your mother and your house?”
sentences.n: ἦ opens a yes-or-no question; it is not ἤ 'or'. ἰθύς 'straight, directly' takes the genitives σῆς μητρός and σοῖο δόμοιο; σῆς and σοῖο 'your', the second a genitive in -οιο; ἴω is the deliberative subjunctive again. This unit closes Theoclymenus’s speech; the closing quotation mark is here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A reply-formula: τὸν 'him' is a pronoun, αὖ 'in turn', ἀντίον 'face to face' an adverb, and ηὔδα the imperfect of αὐδάω 'speak'. πεπνυμένος 'prudent' is Telemachus’s standing epithet.

sentences.t:
ἄλλως μέν σ’ ἂν ἐγώ γε καὶ ἡμέτερόνδε κελοίμην
ἔρχεσθ’·
sentences.tr:
allōs men s’ an egō ge kai hēmeteronde keloimēn
erchesth’·
sentences.l:
“In other circumstances, I at least would bid you even to our house
to come;
sentences.i: “In other circumstances I would myself bid you come even to our house;
sentences.n: Telemachus answers; the speech runs to line 524. ἄλλως 'otherwise, in other circumstances' is explained in what follows. ἂν … κελοίμην 'I would bid' is the optative with ἄν; σ’ is σε; ἐγώ γε 'I at least'. καὶ ἡμέτερόνδε 'even to our house' has the suffix -δε, 'to our (house)'. ἔρχεσθ’ is ἔρχεσθαι with its -αι elided, the infinitive after κελοίμην. The unit ends in the middle of line 514.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ τι ξενίων ποθή·
sentences.tr: ou gar ti xeniōn pothē·
sentences.l: for not at all of hospitality is there a want;
sentences.i: for there is no lack of hospitality;
sentences.n: γάρ explains why Telemachus would in the ordinary way send him to his own house: it would not be wanting in welcome. ξενίων is the genitive plural of ξένια 'the things due a guest, hospitality'; ποθή 'longing, want' is from ποθέω 'miss'; οὐ … ποθή 'there is no want'. Peiraeus says the same thing at 546, with ἔσται. The unit begins in the middle of line 514.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σοὶ αὐτῷ
χεῖρον, ἐπεί τοι ἐγὼ μὲν ἀπέσσομαι, οὐδέ σε μήτηρ
ὄψεται·
sentences.tr:
alla soi autōi
cheiron, epei toi egō men apessomai, oude se mētēr
opsetai·
sentences.i: but it is worse for you yourself, since I shall be away and my mother will not see you;
sentences.n: χεῖρον 'worse' is the neuter comparative of κακός, with ἐστί understood. τοι is the particle ('you see') or the dative σοι; the sense is the same. ἀπέσσομαι is the future of ἄπειμι 'be away' (ἀπο- with ἔσσομαι, the epic future of εἰμί). οὐδέ σε μήτηρ ὄψεται 'nor will (my) mother see you'; ὄψεται is the future of ὁράω. The unit begins in the middle of line 514 and ends in the middle of line 516.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ τι θαμὰ μνηστῆρσ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
φαίνεται, ἀλλ’ ἀπὸ τῶν ὑπερωΐῳ ἱστὸν ὑφαίνει.
sentences.tr:
ou men gar ti thama mnēstērs’ eni oikōi
phainetai, all’ apo tōn hyperōïōi histon hyphainei.
sentences.l:
for not at all often among the suitors in the house
she appears, but apart from them in the upper room a loom she weaves.
sentences.i: for she does not often appear in the house among the suitors, but weaves at her loom in an upper room, away from them.
sentences.n: The subject is Telemachus’s mother, not named. οὐ μὲν γάρ τι 'for not at all'; θαμά 'often'. μνηστῆρσ’ is μνηστῆρσι, the dative plural of μνηστήρ 'suitor', with ἐνὶ οἴκῳ 'in the house'. ἀπὸ τῶν 'apart from them': ἀπό takes the genitive τῶν, the suitors. ὑπερωΐῳ 'in the upper room' is a dative of place (ὑπερῷον). ἱστὸν ὑφαίνει 'weaves at the loom': ἱστός is the upright loom or the web on it, the same word as 'mast' at 496. The unit begins in the middle of line 516.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά τοι ἄλλον φῶτα πιφαύσκομαι ὅν κεν ἵκοιο,
Εὐρύμαχον, Πολύβοιο δαΐφρονος ἀγλαὸν υἱόν,
τὸν νῦν ἶσα θεῷ Ἰθακήσιοι εἰσορόωσι·
sentences.tr:
alla toi allon phōta piphauskomai hon ken hikoio,
Eurymachon, Polyboio daïphronos aglaon huion,
ton nyn isa theōi Ithakēsioi eisoroōsi·
sentences.i: But I point you to another man whom you might visit, Eurymachus, the splendid son of wise-hearted Polybus, whom the Ithacans now look upon as the equal of a god;
sentences.n: τοι is σοι 'to you'. πιφαύσκομαι is a reduplicated form of the verb meaning 'make known', 'I point out'. ὅν κεν ἵκοιο is a relative clause with κε and the optative, 'whom you could go to' (ἱκνέομαι takes an accusative of the person reached); Εὐρύμαχον stands in apposition to φῶτα 'man'. Πολύβοιο is the epic genitive of Πόλυβος. δαΐφρονος 'wise-minded' takes δαΐφρων as formed from δαῆναι 'learn'; the other derivation, from δαίω 'burn', is possible, so the sense is not certain. ἀγλαός 'splendid', here said of a son. τὸν νῦν ἶσα θεῷ: ἶσα is an adverb 'equally' and θεῷ a dative 'to a god', so 'equal to a god'. Ἰθακήσιοι 'Ithacans'; εἰσορόωσι is the uncontracted εἰσοράουσι 'look upon, regard'.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ πολλὸν ἄριστος ἀνὴρ μέμονέν τε μάλιστα
μητέρ’ ἐμὴν γαμέειν καὶ Ὀδυσσῆος γέρας ἕξειν.
sentences.tr:
kai gar pollon aristos anēr memonen te malista
mēter’ emēn gameein kai Odyssēos geras hexein.
sentences.l:
for indeed by far the best man he is, and he is most eager
my mother to marry and Odysseus’ prize to hold.
sentences.i: for he is by far the best man, and he is the most eager to marry my mother and to have the prize of honour that was Odysseus’.
sentences.n: καὶ γάρ 'for indeed' gives the reason. πολλόν is πολύ 'by far', with the superlative ἄριστος 'best'. μέμονε is the perfect of an old verb with present sense, 'is eager, is bent on', with the infinitive γαμέειν, the uncontracted form of γαμεῖν 'marry'. Ὀδυσσῆος γέρας 'Odysseus’ prize' is the honour that belongs to a king; the phrase makes marriage with his wife a claim on his standing. ἕξειν is the future infinitive of ἔχω 'have, hold'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τά γε Ζεὺς οἶδεν Ὀλύμπιος, αἰθέρι ναίων,
εἴ κέ σφι πρὸ γάμοιο τελευτήσει κακὸν ἦμαρ.
sentences.tr:
alla ta ge Zeus oiden Olympios, aitheri naiōn,
ei ke sphi pro gamoio teleutēsei kakon ēmar.
sentences.l:
But these things Zeus knows, Olympian, in the aether dwelling,
whether before the marriage an evil day will come to pass for them.”
sentences.i: But these things Olympian Zeus knows, who dwells in the bright upper air: whether an evil day will come upon them before the marriage.”
sentences.n: τά γε 'these things'. Ζεὺς … Ὀλύμπιος 'Olympian Zeus' has the adjective set after the name; αἰθέρι ναίων 'dwelling in the aether', αἰθήρ being the bright upper air and ναίων the participle of ναίω 'dwell'. εἴ κε with the future τελευτήσει is an indirect question, 'whether'. σφι is the epic dative 'for them', the suitors; πρὸ γάμοιο 'before the marriage', γάμοιο the epic genitive. κακὸν ἦμαρ 'an evil day' is neuter, so it could be the subject (the day will come to pass) or the object (he will bring it about), since τελευτάω can mean either; the English reads it as the subject. The closing quotation mark of Telemachus’s speech is here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα οἱ εἰπόντι ἐπέπτατο δεξιὸς ὄρνις,
κίρκος, Ἀπόλλωνος ταχὺς ἄγγελος·
sentences.tr:
hōs ara hoi eiponti epeptato dexios ornis,
kirkos, Apollōnos tachys angelos·
sentences.l:
So then, to him as he spoke, there flew up on the right a bird,
a falcon, Apollo’s swift messenger;
sentences.i: As soon as he had spoken, a bird flew up on the right, a falcon, the swift messenger of Apollo;
sentences.n: Murray begins a new paragraph; the first line is found elsewhere in the poem, where the bird is an eagle. ἐπέπτατο is the aorist of ἐπιπέτομαι 'fly up'; οἱ εἰπόντι is a dative, 'to him having spoken'. δεξιός 'on the right' is the lucky side for an omen. κίρκος 'falcon' stands in apposition to ὄρνις 'bird'; Ἀπόλλωνος ταχὺς ἄγγελος 'Apollo’s swift messenger' says the bird belongs to the god. The unit ends in the middle of line 526.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ πόδεσσι
τίλλε πέλειαν ἔχων, κατὰ δὲ πτερὰ χεῦεν ἔραζε
μεσσηγὺς νηός τε καὶ αὐτοῦ Τηλεμάχοιο.
sentences.tr:
en de podessi
tille peleian echōn, kata de ptera cheuen eraze
messēgys nēos te kai autou Tēlemachoio.
sentences.l:
and in its feet
it was plucking a dove, holding it, and down it poured the feathers to the ground
between the ship and Telemachus himself.
sentences.i: it was plucking a dove that it held in its feet, and it shed the feathers down to the ground between the ship and Telemachus himself.
sentences.n: ἐν … πόδεσσι 'in its feet' is ἐν with a dative in -εσσι, with δέ standing between them; τίλλε is the imperfect of τίλλω 'pluck'; πέλειαν 'a dove, a rock-pigeon'; ἔχων 'holding'. κατὰ … χεῦεν is tmesis: χεῦεν is the unaugmented aorist of χέω 'pour', so 'poured down, shed'. πτερά 'feathers'; ἔραζε 'to the ground', with the suffix -ζε. μεσσηγύς 'in between' takes the genitives νηός 'the ship' and Τηλεμάχοιο, an epic genitive; αὐτοῦ 'himself'. The feathers land right in front of Telemachus. The unit begins in the middle of line 526.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ Θεοκλύμενος ἑτάρων ἀπονόσφι καλέσσας
ἔν τ’ ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρὶ ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.tr:
ton de Theoklymenos hetarōn aponosphi kalessas
en t’ ara hoi phy cheiri epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomaze·
sentences.l:
And him Theoclymenus, apart from his companions having called,
clasped by the hand, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: Theoclymenus called him aside, away from his companions, took his hand, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: τὸν 'him' is Telemachus. ἑτάρων ἀπονόσφι 'apart from his companions' (ἀπονόσφι takes the genitive); καλέσσας is the aorist participle of καλέω 'call'. ἔν τ’ ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρί: ἔν … φῦ is tmesis, φῦ being the aorist (ἔφυ) of φύω 'grow', so 'grew into' for 'clung to, clasped'; οἱ is 'to him' and χειρί 'by the hand'. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε 'and spoke a word, and called him by name' is a stock line for a speaker who takes the hearer’s hand; ἔκ … ὀνόμαζε is tmesis for ἐξωνόμαζε 'name, address by name'.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, οὔ τοι ἄνευ θεοῦ ἔπτατο δεξιὸς ὄρνις
ἔγνων γάρ μιν ἐσάντα ἰδὼν οἰωνὸν ἐόντα.
sentences.tr:
Tēlemach’, ou toi aneu theou eptato dexios ornis
egnōn gar min esanta idōn oiōnon eonta.
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, not without a god flew the bird on the right;
for I knew it, face to face having seen it, to be a bird of omen.
sentences.i: “Telemachus, that bird did not fly up on the right without a god; for I knew, when I saw it right before me, that it was a bird of omen.
sentences.n: Theoclymenus speaks; the speech runs to line 534. οὔ τοι 'surely not' (τοι appeals to the hearer). ἄνευ θεοῦ 'without a god', that is, not by chance. ἔπτατο is the aorist of πέτομαι 'fly'; δεξιὸς ὄρνις 'a bird on the right'. ἔγνων γάρ 'for I recognised'; μιν 'it' is the bird, and οἰωνὸν ἐόντα 'being a bird of omen' is a participle (ἐόντα = ὄντα) after ἔγνων; ἐσάντα 'right opposite, face to face'; ἰδών is the aorist participle of ὁράω.

sentences.t:
ὑμετέρου δ’ οὐκ ἔστι γένος βασιλεύτερον ἄλλο
ἐν δήμῳ Ἰθάκης, ἀλλ’ ὑμεῖς καρτεροὶ αἰεί.
sentences.tr:
hymeterou d’ ouk esti genos basileuteron allo
en dēmōi Ithakēs, all’ hymeis karteroi aiei.
sentences.l:
Than yours there is not another family more kingly
in the land of Ithaca, but you are strong always.”
sentences.i: No other family in the land of Ithaca is more kingly than yours; you are strong always.”
sentences.n: ὑμετέρου 'than yours' is a genitive of comparison, standing for 'than your family', after βασιλεύτερον 'more kingly', the comparative of βασιλεύς 'king'; γένος 'family, stock' is the subject of οὐκ ἔστι. ἄλλο 'other'; ἐν δήμῳ Ἰθάκης 'in the land of Ithaca' (δῆμος 'district, land'). ἀλλά 'but'; ὑμεῖς καρτεροί 'you are strong' (καρτερός, the epic form of κρατερός), with αἰεί 'always', the epic form of ἀεί. The closing quotation mark of Theoclymenus’s speech is here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: The same reply-formula as at line 512, with the same English.

sentences.t: αἲ γὰρ τοῦτο, ξεῖνε, ἔπος τετελεσμένον εἴη·
sentences.tr: ai gar touto, xeine, epos tetelesmenon eiē·
sentences.l: “Would that this, stranger, word fulfilled might be;
sentences.i: “If only this word of yours, stranger, might be fulfilled;
sentences.n: Telemachus answers; the speech runs to line 538. αἲ γάρ 'would that' opens a wish, with the optative εἴη 'may it be'. ξεῖνε 'stranger'. ἔπος τετελεσμένον 'a word fulfilled' has τετελεσμένον, the perfect passive participle of τελέω 'fulfil'; the word is Theoclymenus’s reading of the omen.

sentences.t:
τῷ κε τάχα γνοίης φιλότητά τε πολλά τε δῶρα
ἐξ ἐμεῦ, ὡς ἄν τίς σε συναντόμενος μακαρίζοι.
sentences.tr:
tōi ke tacha gnoiēs philotēta te polla te dōra
ex emeu, hōs an tis se synantomenos makarizoi.
sentences.l:
then soon you would know friendship and many gifts
from me, so that someone meeting you would call you blessed.”
sentences.i: Then you would soon know friendship from me, and many gifts, so that anyone who met you would call you blessed.”
sentences.n: τῷ 'then, in that case' is an old instrumental of the pronoun. κε with the optative γνοίης (aorist of γιγνώσκω) 'you would come to know'; τάχα 'soon'. φιλότητα 'friendship' and πολλά τε δῶρα 'and many gifts' are both objects; ἐξ ἐμεῦ 'from me', ἐμεῦ being the epic genitive of ἐγώ. ὡς ἄν with the optative μακαρίζοι 'so that … would call blessed' is a purpose clause; τίς 'someone, anyone'; συναντόμενος 'meeting (you)'. The closing quotation mark of Telemachus’s speech is here.

sentences.t: ἦ καὶ Πείραιον προσεφώνεε, πιστὸν ἑταῖρον·
sentences.tr: ē kai Peiraion prosephōnee, piston hetairon·
sentences.l: He spoke, and to Peiraeus spoke, his faithful companion:
sentences.i: So he said, and spoke to Peiraeus, his faithful companion:
sentences.n: The speaker is Telemachus, who has just finished speaking to Theoclymenus and now turns to one of his own crew. ἦ καί 'he spoke, and' uses ἦ, the old imperfect of ἠμί 'say'. προσεφώνεε is the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω 'speak to, call to'. Πείραιον is the accusative of Πείραιος; πιστὸν ἑταῖρον 'a faithful companion', πιστός 'faithful' being from the root of πείθω.

sentences.t:
Πείραιε Κλυτίδη, σὺ δέ μοι τά περ ἄλλα μάλιστα
πείθῃ ἐμῶν ἑτάρων, οἵ μοι Πύλον εἰς ἅμ’ ἕποντο·
sentences.tr:
Peiraie Klytidē, sy de moi ta per alla malista
peithēi emōn hetarōn, hoi moi Pylon eis ham’ heponto·
sentences.l:
“Peiraeus, son of Clytius, you in the other matters most of all
obey me of my companions, who to Pylos together followed me;
sentences.i: “Peiraeus, son of Clytius, in other matters you obey me more than any of my companions who followed me to Pylos;
sentences.n: Telemachus speaks to Peiraeus; the speech runs to line 543. Κλυτίδη is the vocative of Κλυτίδης 'son of Clytius'. σὺ δέ 'and you'; μοι 'to me', with πείθῃ, which is πείθεαι, second person middle, 'you obey'. τά περ ἄλλα 'in the other matters' is an accusative of respect, with περ 'just'; μάλιστα 'most'; ἐμῶν ἑτάρων 'of my companions' is partitive. οἵ … ἕποντο is a relative clause: ἕποντο is the unaugmented (= εἵποντο) imperfect of ἕπομαι 'follow'; Πύλον εἰς is εἰς Πύλον, with the preposition after its noun; ἅμ’ is ἅμα 'along with'.

sentences.t:
καὶ νῦν μοι τὸν ξεῖνον ἄγων ἐν δώμασι σοῖσιν
ἐνδυκέως φιλέειν καὶ τιέμεν, εἰς ὅ κεν ἔλθω.
sentences.tr:
kai nyn moi ton xeinon agōn en dōmasi soisin
endykeōs phileein kai tiemen, eis ho ken elthō.
sentences.l:
and now, for me, the stranger leading to your house
kindly to befriend and to honour, until I come.”
sentences.i: and now take the stranger to your house for me, treat him as a friend, kindly, and honour him until I come.”
sentences.n: καὶ νῦν 'and now too'; μοι 'for me' is a dative of interest, 'please'. ἄγων 'leading'; ἐν δώμασι σοῖσιν 'in your house', with σοῖσιν the possessive in -οισιν. φιλέειν (the uncontracted φιλεῖν) and τιέμεν (the infinitive of τίω 'honour' in its -έμεν form) are infinitives used as commands, 'treat as a friend and honour'; ἐνδυκέως 'kindly'. εἰς ὅ κεν ἔλθω 'until I come' is κε with the aorist subjunctive. The closing quotation mark of Telemachus’s speech is here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Πείραιος δουρικλυτὸς ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Peiraios douriklytos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn Peiraeus, famed-for-the-spear, spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Peiraeus, famed for his spear, spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This is the reply-formula of 512 and 535 with Peiraeus’s name and epithet in place of Telemachus’s. δουρικλυτός 'famed for the spear' joins δόρυ 'spear' to κλυτός 'famous'; it is the same compound as δουρικλειτός, and is translated the same way each time.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, εἰ γάρ κεν σὺ πολὺν χρόνον ἐνθάδε μίμνοι,
τόνδε τ’ ἐγὼ κομιῶ, ξενίων δέ οἱ οὐ ποθὴ ἔσται.
sentences.tr:
Tēlemach’, ei gar ken sy polyn chronon enthade mimnoi,
tonde t’ egō komiō, xeniōn de hoi ou pothē estai.
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, for if you a long time here should stay,
this man I will look after, and of hospitality for him no want will be.”
sentences.i: “Telemachus, even if you stay here a long time, I will look after this man, and for him there will be no lack of hospitality.”
sentences.n: Peiraeus answers; this is his whole speech. εἰ γάρ κεν … μίμνοι 'for if … you should stay' is a conditional clause (εἰ with κε and the optative of μίμνω, a form of μένω); the force is 'even if', since he promises to look after the guest however long Telemachus is away. πολὺν χρόνον 'a long time'; ἐνθάδε 'here'. τόνδε 'this man'; κομιῶ is the future of κομίζω 'look after, take care of'. ξενίων … ποθὴ ἔσται 'there will be no want of hospitality' repeats the phrase of 514 with ἔσται 'will be'; οἱ 'for him'.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἐπὶ νηὸς ἔβη, ἐκέλευσε δ’ ἑταίρους
αὐτούς τ’ ἀμβαίνειν ἀνά τε πρυμνήσια λῦσαι.
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn epi nēos ebē, ekeleuse d’ hetairous
autous t’ ambainein ana te prymnēsia lysai.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, onto the ship he went, and he ordered his companions
themselves to embark and to loose the stern-cables.
sentences.i: So saying, he went on board and ordered his companions themselves to embark and to cast off the stern-cables.
sentences.n: Murray begins a new paragraph; the second line is found elsewhere in the poem, with the same English. ὣς εἰπών 'so having spoken'; ἐπὶ νηὸς ἔβη 'went on to the ship', ἐπί with the genitive. ἐκέλευσε 'ordered' takes the accusative ἑταίρους 'companions' and the infinitives. The subject is Peiraeus; αὐτούς 'themselves' is the men, set against Peiraeus, who has gone aboard first. ἀμβαίνειν is ἀναβαίνειν 'go aboard' with the α of ἀνα- dropped and the ν assimilated to β; ἀνά … λῦσαι is tmesis for ἀναλῦσαι 'loose'; πρυμνήσια 'stern-cables'.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ αἶψ’ εἴσβαινον καὶ ἐπὶ κληῗσι καθῖζον.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ aips’ eisbainon kai epi klēïsi kathizon.
sentences.l: and they quickly went aboard and on the rowing-benches sat down.
sentences.i: and they quickly went aboard and sat down on the rowing-benches.
sentences.n: εἴσβαινον is the imperfect of εἰσβαίνω 'go aboard', without its augment. κληῗσι is the dative plural of κληΐς, the diaeresis marking the ι as a syllable of its own after η; the word first means 'bar, key', and in a ship the rowing-benches or thwarts, the exact timber being unsettled. καθῖζον is the imperfect of καθίζω 'sit down'.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δ’ ὑπὸ ποσσὶν ἐδήσατο καλὰ πέδιλα,
εἵλετο δ’ ἄλκιμον ἔγχος, ἀκαχμένον ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
νηὸς ἀπ’ ἰκριόφιν·
sentences.tr:
Tēlemachos d’ hypo possin edēsato kala pedila,
heileto d’ alkimon enchos, akachmenon oxeï chalkōi,
nēos ap’ ikriophin·
sentences.i: Telemachus bound fair sandals under his feet and took up a sturdy spear, pointed with sharp bronze, from the deck of the ship;
sentences.n: ἐδήσατο 'bound on (for himself)' is the aorist middle of δέω; ὑπὸ ποσσίν 'under his feet', ποσσί being the dative plural of πούς; πέδιλα 'sandals'. εἵλετο 'took up' is the aorist middle of αἱρέω; ἄλκιμον 'sturdy' comes from ἀλκή 'strength in fight'; ἔγχος 'spear'. ἀκαχμένον is the perfect passive participle of a verb from the root ἀκ- 'point, sharp', 'pointed' (a different word from ἀκαχήμενος 'grieved' at 481); ὀξέϊ is the dative of ὀξύς 'sharp', and χαλκῷ 'bronze' a dative of means. ἰκριόφιν is a form in -φιν, 'from the deck', from ἴκρια 'decking'. The unit ends in the middle of line 552.

sentences.t: τοὶ δὲ πρυμνήσι’ ἔλυσαν.
sentences.tr: toi de prymnēsi’ elysan.
sentences.l: and they loosed the stern-cables.
sentences.i: and they cast off the stern-cables.
sentences.n: τοί is the old form of the pronoun οἱ, 'they', here the crew; ἔλυσαν 'loosed' is the aorist of λύω; πρυμνήσι’ is πρυμνήσια. The unit begins in the middle of line 552.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἀνώσαντες πλέον ἐς πόλιν, ὡς ἐκέλευσε
Τηλέμαχος, φίλος υἱὸς Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο·
sentences.tr:
hoi men anōsantes pleon es polin, hōs ekeleuse
Tēlemachos, philos huios Odyssēos theioio·
sentences.l:
They, having pushed off, sailed to the city, as ordered
Telemachus, dear son of Odysseus, divine;
sentences.i: Pushing off, they sailed to the city, as Telemachus, the dear son of divine Odysseus, had ordered;
sentences.n: οἱ μέν 'they, for their part' is the crew, answered by τὸν δέ 'and him' in the next line. ἀνώσαντες is the aorist participle of ἀνωθέω 'push (the ship) off'; πλέον 'were sailing'; ἐς πόλιν 'to the city'; ὡς ἐκέλευσε 'as he ordered'. The name comes after the verb, with its full line-end epithet: Τηλέμαχος, φίλος υἱὸς Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο 'Telemachus, dear son of divine Odysseus'. θείοιο is the epic genitive of θεῖος 'divine'; the line is found elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ὦκα προβιβάντα πόδες φέρον, ὄφρ’ ἵκετ’ αὐλήν,
ἔνθα οἱ ἦσαν ὕες μάλα μυρίαι, ᾗσι συβώτης
ἐσθλὸς ἐὼν ἐνίαυεν, ἀνάκτεσιν ἤπια εἰδώς.
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ōka probibanta podes pheron, ophr’ hiket’ aulēn,
entha hoi ēsan hyes mala myriai, hēisi sybōtēs
esthlos eōn eniauen, anaktesin ēpia eidōs.
sentences.l:
and him quickly, striding forward, his feet bore, until he came to the courtyard,
where for him were swine very numberless, among which the swineherd
being good slept, to his lords kindly things knowing.
sentences.i: And his feet carried him quickly forward until he reached the yard, where the swineherd had swine beyond counting; among them he used to sleep, a good man, kindly disposed to his lords.
sentences.n: τὸν 'him' is Telemachus. προβιβάντα is the accusative participle of προβαίνω (the epic βιβάω form) 'stepping forward', agreeing with τὸν; πόδες φέρον 'his feet bore him' makes the feet the subject. ὄφρ’ ἵκετ’ αὐλήν 'until he came to the yard': ὄφρα 'until', ἵκετ’ the aorist of ἱκνέομαι. αὐλή is the courtyard of the steading. ἔνθα οἱ ἦσαν ὕες 'where there were swine for him': οἱ looks ahead to the swineherd named in the relative clause. ὕες is the plural of ὗς 'swine'; μάλα μυρίαι 'very numberless'. ᾗσι is a dative plural feminine relative, 'among which'. συβώτης 'swineherd'; ἐσθλὸς ἐών 'being good', ἐών = ὤν; ἐνίαυεν is the imperfect of ἰαύω 'sleep, lodge'. ἀνάκτεσιν is the dative plural of ἄναξ 'lord', 'to his lords'; ἤπια εἰδώς 'knowing kindly things' means being kindly disposed.
